$note: BroGram lessons. One lesson per CLO. No institution names, no pattern ids, no emoji.

lessons.title: From Functions to Classes
lessons.hook: Same program, but now the data finally lives where it's used.

blocks.heading: One Class, One Job
blocks.body: When you write procedural code, you keep data in loose variables and pass them into separate functions that live on their own. Nothing forces your data and the code that changes it to stay together, so it's easy to lose track of which function is allowed to touch which variable. Object-oriented code fixes that by bundling data and the methods that act on it into one unit: a class. Every object you create from a class carries its own copy of that data, plus the methods allowed to change it. Rewriting a procedural program as classes means finding the data that travels together and giving it a home.

blocks.caption: Static example, no Run button here. Same idea: the name and the behavior that uses it travel together in one object.

steps.say: Player bundles the name and score together -- one object, not two variables floating separately.
The constructor sets initial state right when the object is created, so score always starts clean.
addPoints is a method on Player, not a standalone function -- it changes the object's own score directly.
Creating a Player object gives you one thing to pass around, instead of juggling separate name and score variables.
You read score straight off the object -- no separate function needed to fetch it.

blocks.caption: A running score rewritten as a class instead of a loose variable.

blocks.prompt: A procedural version of Player would keep name and score as separate variables and pass them into standalone functions. What's the real difference once you switch to the class version above?
options: The class version bundles score with the method that changes it, so a Player carries its own behavior.
The class version runs faster because Java optimizes classes automatically.
The class version needs no constructor because Java creates default values for every field.
The class version can only be used once, while procedural functions can be reused.
why: Right -- the object owns its own data and the method that updates it.
Speed is not the point; the code does the same work either way.
The class still needs a constructor to set score for you -- you wrote one above.
You can create as many Player objects as you want; that's part of the value.
blocks.hint: Look at what lives inside Player versus what used to be separate variables and functions.
blocks.explain: Grouping score and addPoints inside Player means the object always knows how to change its own state, instead of a function reaching in from outside.

blocks.prompt: Finish the Rectangle class below so width and height get stored, and area() returns their product. main already builds a Rectangle from two numbers typed in and prints its area.
blocks.hint: Assign the constructor's w and h into width and height, then multiply width by height in area().
blocks.explain: The constructor's job is to save incoming state on the object; area() then just reads that state back arithmetically -- that's the whole shift from loose variables to a class.

bullets: Procedural code passes data between separate functions.
OOP bundles data and the methods that change it into one class.
A constructor sets an object's starting state the moment it's built.
blocks.remember: If data and the function that changes it always travel together, make them a class.

blocks.say: Time to turn a real procedural mess into your own class -- a real one's next.

lessons.exitLine: Time to turn a real procedural mess into your own class -- a real one's next.

lessons.title: Sketch it before you code it
lessons.hook: Get the boxes right on paper, and the class file basically writes itself.

blocks.heading: Sketch the classes before you code
blocks.body: Before you open an editor, sketch the classes on paper first. That sketch has a standard notation, UML: one box per class, its fields listed inside, lines connecting boxes that need each other. A line between two boxes means one class holds a reference to the other — a has-a relationship, called an association. An open arrow from a smaller box up to a bigger one means the smaller class inherits everything the bigger one has — an is-a relationship. Decide which kind each connection is first. Then coding becomes translation, not invention: each box becomes a class, each listed field becomes a class field, and each line becomes either a stored reference or an extends clause.

blocks.caption: Static example, no Run button here. Square is-a Shape (extends). Drawing has-a Shape (a stored field). Same two relationships, side by side.

steps.say: Fields here are exactly the attributes the sketch listed — nothing invented while coding.
This extends mirrors the inheritance arrow directly — every field and method Vehicle has, Car now gets.
One class holding a reference to another class is what an association line meant on paper.
The constructor sets up that association once, so every method afterward can rely on it existing.
Calling vehicle.costFor(days) proves the association works — Rental leans on Vehicle instead of repeating its math.

blocks.caption: Every box from the sketch becomes a class; every connecting line becomes a field or an extends clause.

blocks.prompt: A Team class keeps a list of Player objects it manages. A Goalkeeper class extends Player and adds nothing else. Which pair of words correctly labels the two relationships?
options: Team has-a Player; Goalkeeper is-a Player
Team is-a Player; Goalkeeper has-a Player
Team has-a Player; Goalkeeper has-a Player
Team is-a Player; Goalkeeper is-a Player
why: Right — a stored list is a reference, so that is has-a, and extends is inheritance, so that is is-a.
Backwards — a stored list is an association, not inheritance, and extends is inheritance, not an association.
Team is right, but extends always means is-a, never has-a, no matter what the subclass adds.
A stored list is never inheritance — Team only holds Player objects, it does not extend Player.
blocks.hint: Look at what each relationship actually does: does one class extend the other, or just keep a reference to it?
blocks.explain: Team stores a list of Player references, so that is has-a — an association. Goalkeeper extends Player, so that is is-a — inheritance. Same two relationship types as the sketch, applied to a new pair of classes.

blocks.prompt: Finish Dog so a dog prints "Rex barks" while any other animal still prints "Milo makes a sound" — using a constructor and an override, not a new field. Main already reads the kind and the name for you.
blocks.hint: Give Dog a constructor that calls super(name), then override speak() to return something different from Animal's version.
blocks.explain: Dog's constructor passes name up with super(name), and overriding speak() lets the same call, a.speak(), produce a different result depending on the actual object — exactly what an is-a relationship promises.

bullets: Boxes on paper become classes; fields on paper become fields.
A stored reference is has-a; extends is is-a.
Code should mirror the sketch exactly, not improve on it while typing.
blocks.remember: Design the relationships first — has-a or is-a — then let the code follow.

blocks.say: Next you sketch a structure yourself, then build it in code without drifting from that sketch.

lessons.exitLine: Go sketch the next one first — then make the code match it exactly.

lessons.title: One Call, Different Bodies
lessons.hook: One line of code, and the object underneath decides what actually happens.

blocks.heading: One Call, The Object Decides
blocks.body: When a subclass overrides a method — same name, same parameters, same return type — you can call it through a variable declared as the superclass. Java still runs the subclass's version, not the superclass's. The declared type only limits which methods you are allowed to call; the actual object decides which body executes. That means one line of code, written once against the superclass, behaves differently depending on what object you hand it. Mark the subclass method @Override so the compiler checks it truly replaces a matching superclass method, instead of quietly creating an unrelated one because a parameter or the name did not match exactly.

blocks.caption: Static example, no Run button here. i is typed Instrument, but the object underneath is a Guitar.

steps.say: A default bonus here means every Employee responds to the same call, even before overriding exists.
Same name and return type let this replace Employee's version instead of hiding beside it.
Typing the list as Employee lets Sam and Rae share one collection despite being different classes.
e is typed Employee, but Java still runs whichever bonus() the real object defines.

blocks.caption: Two classes, one loop — the object each slot holds decides which bonus prints.

blocks.prompt: notify(n) only ever sees n as a Notification. What does this print?
blocks.hint: notify's parameter type never changes. Ask what each array slot actually holds instead.
blocks.explain: notify always receives something typed Notification, but the first slot really is a plain Notification and the second really is an UrgentNotification, so send() resolves separately for each one: ping, then ALERT.

blocks.prompt: computeTotal(Discount d, double amount) returns amount * (1 - d.rate()). Discount.rate() returns 0.05; VipDiscount overrides rate() to return 0.2. discounts is a Discount[] where index 0 holds a plain Discount and index 1 holds a VipDiscount. What does computeTotal(discounts[1], 250) return?
options: 200.0, because the object at index 1 is really a VipDiscount, whatever type the array or parameter is declared as
237.5, because the array and the parameter are both typed Discount, so rate() always resolves to Discount's own version
A compile error, because a VipDiscount cannot be stored in a Discount[]
It depends on the order the discounts were added to the array
why: Right. The object at index 1 really is a VipDiscount, so its own rate() runs: 250 * (1 - 0.2) = 200.0, no matter how the parameter is declared.
That would only be true if overriding did not exist. The declared type never decides which body runs — the actual object always does.
A VipDiscount is a Discount, so storing it in a Discount[] compiles and runs fine; that is the entire reason to type the array as the supertype.
Insertion order never changes which method a given object runs. Only the object's own type decides that.
blocks.hint: Look at what discounts[1] actually is, not what the array or the parameter is typed as.
blocks.explain: computeTotal takes a Discount, but discounts[1] is really a VipDiscount, so d.rate() runs VipDiscount's overridden version: 250 * (1 - 0.2) = 200.0. The declared type Discount only controls which methods are callable, never which body executes.

bullets: Overriding keeps the method name, replacing the superclass's version entirely.
The declared type limits calls; the real object picks the method.
One call site, many bodies, decided only by the object you pass.
blocks.remember: The object decides which body runs, never the variable's label.

blocks.say: Next you write the override yourself, on a class you have not seen yet.

lessons.exitLine: Same call, different body, decided entirely by the object underneath.

lessons.title: Swap Behavior, Not Code
lessons.hook: Same call, different move - that's the whole trick.

blocks.heading: Pick behavior at runtime
blocks.body: When a class must behave differently depending on context, avoid a growing if/else inside it. Instead, define a small interface with one method - the behavior. Write each option as its own class implementing that interface. The class needing the behavior stores a reference to the interface, never to one concrete option, and calls that single method. To change behavior, hand it a different object; nothing inside the class changes. This is the strategy pattern: pick the algorithm at runtime by swapping objects, not editing code. It keeps a class open to new behavior later without touching what already works.

blocks.caption: Static example, no Run button here. Same call, different sound - swap the object, not the class.

steps.say: One shared method means any style can stand in for another without Host knowing which one it got.
Each style is its own small class, so a new one never edits the others.
Host keeps a reference to the interface, never to one style, so it stays unchanged later.
Choosing Formal happens only here - the one place behavior actually gets picked for this run.
Swapping to Casual needs only a new object, proof Host never changed to allow it.

blocks.caption: Same Host, two voices - nothing about Host changes.

blocks.prompt: Same idea, new channels. Trace which object each call goes through before you predict what prints, in order.
blocks.hint: Look at which object n holds at the moment each alert call actually runs, not which one it started with.
blocks.explain: n is reassigned to a new Notifier before the second alert, so the second line comes from Email, not Sms.

blocks.prompt: A payment class picks its logic with a five-branch if/else instead of separate classes behind one interface. What's the real cost of leaving it that way?
options: Every new payment type means editing that one class and risking the branches that already work.
The code runs slower because if/else is slower than calling an interface method.
Java won't compile a class once it has more than a few if/else branches.
Nothing changes - if/else and separate classes behave identically either way.
why: Right - every new option touches shared code, so one mistake can break a branch that already shipped.
Speed isn't the issue here; both approaches run in about the same time for this kind of logic.
Java has no branch limit - this fails for a design reason, not a compiler one.
They can produce the same output, but only one of them keeps changes contained to new code.
blocks.hint: Think about what you'd have to touch in that one class to add a sixth payment type.
blocks.explain: The interface version adds a class; the if/else version edits a class that already worked and already shipped.

bullets: One interface, many classes - behavior swaps by passing a different object.
The caller never touches new options; it only calls the shared method.
Pick this shape when new behavior keeps showing up and edits keep breaking things.
blocks.remember: New behavior gets a new class, never a new branch.

blocks.say: Time to pick this shape yourself on a rep that actually needs it.

lessons.exitLine: One interface, swapped objects - that's the whole move.
